Larimer County in brief

Larimer County lies along the Wyoming border and covers 2,634 square miles. Fort Collins is the seat and largest city. The county counted 359,066 residents in 2020. One tax roll holds city lots, farm parcels and mountain cabins, so what applies to your house depends heavily on where it sits.

Offices that handle property tax

The Assessor values property and takes protests. The Treasurer, who also serves as Public Trustee, mails statements and collects payment. Both offices are at 200 W. Oak Street in Fort Collins.

  • Treasurer and Public Trustee: Suite 2100, (970) 498-7020, open 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., Monday through Friday. Mail goes to P.O. Box 1250, Fort Collins, CO 80522.
  • Assessor: second floor, (970) 498-7050, same weekday hours. Mail goes to P.O. Box 1190.
  • Title companies use the Treasury's CTD login, and mortgage servicers have a mass payment option.

The Treasurer does not determine the amount of tax. Value questions go to the Assessor. The rate comes from the cities, county, schools and districts that tax your address.

How the bill is calculated

Assessed value multiplied by the mill levy gives the tax, and assessed value is actual value times an assessment rate. For 2026, residential property has two rates for the first time: 6.8% for local government and 7.05% for schools.

Your levy depends on every district on your bill, so the county's guide to Colorado property taxes is the place to see the math laid out step by step.

How the county values homes

Real property is revalued in odd-numbered years. Residential values for 2025 and 2026 rest on market conditions at June 30, 2024, using a sales study that ran from July 1, 2022 through June 30, 2024 and covered 24 months. Vacant and commercial land uses 60 months of sales.

Two details matter to sellers. Foreclosure transfers to lenders are left out of the study, though resales of foreclosed homes are generally used. And the Assessor measures square footage from exterior dimensions, so a builder's interior figure may differ from the county record.

In an intervening year such as 2026, Notices of Valuation usually mail only when value or classification changed.

How to protest your valuation

Protests are accepted from May 1 through June 8. File by mail, through an online tool the county puts at 15 minutes or less, in person, by phone or appointment, by fax at 970-498-7070, or at the secure drop box at the southwest entrance of 200 W. Oak Street.

The assessor calendar then runs in this order: Notices of Determination by June 30, County Board of Equalization hearings from July 1 to August 5, and a July 15 deadline to appeal to that board. An alternate protest period comes later, with hearings from September 1 to November 2 and an appeal deadline of September 15.

You can contest only value or classification. Levies belong to the taxing districts, not the Assessor.

Payment options and due dates

Partial payments are not accepted. Amounts of $25 or less are due in full by April 30.

The tax lien sale

Unpaid real property taxes go to a public lien sale. This year's is set for Thursday, November 19, 2026 at the Larimer County Fairgrounds at the Ranch, 5280 Arena Circle, Loveland, with registration at 7:30 a.m. It is held in person, not online.

The 2026 investor rate is 13%, which state law sets as the federal discount rate on September 1 plus nine points. The advertising list goes up online in early October and updates nightly. Tax sale certificates cancel automatically after fifteen years.

Ask the Treasurer for the redemption timing on any lien against your house.

Wildfire history and buyers

The Cameron Peak fire began August 13, 2020 in Roosevelt National Forest and was fully contained December 2, 2020. It burned 208,663 acres and destroyed 469 structures, 42 of them primary residences. A Forest Service report found 36% of the burned land had high soil burn severity, with a high risk of erosion or flooding.

Owners in Poudre Canyon, Red Feather Lakes, Redstone Canyon and Storm Mountain should expect buyers and insurers to ask about burn scars and defensible space.

Who to call about what

Mixing up the two offices is the most common time-waster. Use this as a quick guide.

  • Your house is worth less than the notice says: call the Assessor at (970) 498-7050.
  • You need a payoff, a receipt or a statement: call the Treasurer at (970) 498-7020.
  • A title company needs a Certificate of Taxes Due: it orders through the Treasury's CTD login.
  • An old loan is still on record: the Treasurer also serves as Public Trustee, so the same office can point you to the release process.

If you are not sure which side a question belongs to, start with the Treasurer. Staff there can tell you when the answer sits with the Assessor, since the Treasurer's office does not decide the amount of tax.

Relief programs worth asking about

Owners who struggle with the bill have several options before a lien comes into play. The county lists a senior exemption, a veteran with a disability exemption, a deferral program, a work off program and the property tax, rent and heat rebate. Each has its own rules, so ask the Treasurer which ones fit your situation.

A deferral or an unpaid balance can show up when a buyer's title company searches the property, which is another reason to settle the account before you list. Owners who pay through mortgage escrow should check that the servicer actually sent the money, because a missed escrow payment still becomes a delinquent balance on the county's books.

Back taxes and inherited houses

Common problems are a delinquent bill, a title that needs a probate step, and a roof or foundation that makes a retail listing hard. A cash buyer can take the house as it stands, but a tax lien still gets paid from proceeds at closing. Get a payoff figure from the Treasurer at (970) 498-7020 first.

Plan the steps in order. Request the Certificate of Taxes Due through your title company, ask the Treasurer for a payoff on any delinquent amount, and let the closing company know about any open lien so it can be settled from your proceeds.

Frequently asked questions

When are Larimer County property taxes due?

Taxes are due in two equal installments, at the end of February and June 15, or in one payment by April 30. A date on a non-business day moves to the next business day.

What is the Larimer County property tax protest deadline?

Protests to the Assessor are accepted May 1 through June 8. You can file by mail, online, in person, by phone or fax, or at the drop box at 200 W. Oak Street.

Does Larimer County run its tax lien sale online?

No. This year's sale is in person at the Larimer County Fairgrounds at the Ranch in Loveland on November 19, 2026.

How are Larimer County homes valued for 2026?

2026 is an intervening year, so residential values still reflect the June 30, 2024 appraisal date and a sales study from July 1, 2022 through June 30, 2024.

Who sets my Larimer County tax rate?

Taxing authorities such as cities, the county, school districts and fire districts set levies. The Assessor sets value and the Treasurer collects the bill.

Denver County in brief

There is no second layer of local government in Denver County. On December 1, 1902 the City of Denver merged with Arapahoe County, creating one consolidated city and county that covers 154.7 square miles. Its 78 official neighborhoods grew out of the 1970 statistical neighborhoods, and well-known informal names such as LoDo, RiNo, Park Hill and Central Park, the former Stapleton area, are used alongside them.

You receive a single tax bill here, and the people who value and collect work in the same Department of Finance. The bill lists each taxing authority on your parcel. Two houses a short walk apart may sit in different school or special districts.

Who values and who collects

Value comes from the Assessor and collection from the Treasury division. Neither sets the rate. If a bill seems too high, decide whether the value is off, which the Assessor can review, or the levy is simply high, which only the taxing authority controls.

OfficeWhat it does
Assessor's OfficeValues real property, mails Notices of Valuation, takes protests
TreasuryMails statements, collects payments, runs the delinquent list and tax lien sale
Taxing authoritiesSet mill levies each December

Denver's combined general levy for 2024 was 79.202 mills, or 0.079202.

How Denver values a house

Appraisers compare each house with recent sales of similar homes, and the whole city gets a new appraisal every second year, the odd-numbered ones such as 2023 and 2025. The 2025 values rest on sales from July 1, 2022 through June 30, 2024. Commercial and industrial property uses cost, market and income approaches, and business personal property is valued from what owners declare.

The Assessor's formula: (actual value minus value reduction) times assessment rate times mill levy. For 2024 the inputs were:

  • Residential: $55,000 value reduction per parcel, 6.7% assessment rate.
  • Commercial improved: $30,000 reduction, 27.9% rate.
  • All other: no reduction, 27.9% rate.

Residential property now carries two rates, and the state's 2026 chart lists 6.8% for local government levies and 7.05% for school levies. Your own notice and bill hold the numbers for the year you are in.

Property tax calendar

Expect your statement in January. You can pay half by the last day of February and half by June 15, or pay in full by April 30.

  • By May 1: the Assessor mails Notices of Valuation.
  • May: delinquency notices go to unpaid accounts.
  • September and October: delinquent taxes are advertised in a local newspaper.
  • October: the public auction of real estate tax liens.

The Assessor mails senior citizen and disabled veteran exemption notices in January. Elderly and disabled refund applications are due April 30, and deferral applications for seniors and active-duty military are due April 1.

How to protest a valuation

File by June 8, or the next business day when that date is a weekend or holiday. Instructions arrive with the Assessor's Notice of Valuation, and protests can be written, made in person or sent over the internet. Your protest should have:

  • Your parcel or schedule number from the notice and a daytime phone number.
  • Your reasons, stated plainly.
  • Evidence such as comparable sales or documented condition problems.

Let a year slip by? You can reach back two prior years with a Board of County Commissioners petition for abatement or refund of taxes. A decision you dislike can go to the State Board of Assessment Appeals, to District Court or to binding arbitration. Counties with more than 300,000 residents follow the state's alternate schedule, with Notices of Determination mailed by August 15.

Filing before you list can help. A lower value changes the bill your buyer takes over, and a house with documented repair needs usually argues its case better than one in move-in shape.

Hail and your roof

Storms are frequent enough that the roof is normally the first thing a buyer or inspector brings up. Denver ranks tenth among U.S. cities of 50,000 or more for hail risk, and three of the ten costliest hailstorms in U.S. history struck it, in 1990, 2009 and 2017.

Hail scars, cracked siding and dented gutters cut into a conventional buyer's offer. Selling to a cash buyer who accepts the house as is takes that haggling off the table.

Exemptions, refunds and deferrals

Denver lists several relief programs on its calendar. Senior citizen and disabled veteran exemption notices come from the Assessor in January. The elderly and disabled refund program takes applications until April 30. Seniors and active-duty military can apply for a deferral by April 1, and anyone who is planning to sell should read the repayment terms before applying.

The state records a deferral against the house as a lien. A sale adds its payoff to the closing statement, so request the amount while the house is listed and not the day before you close.

From contract to closing

With a buyer under contract, things move fast. Title orders the payoff and searches for liens, and whatever turns up is itemized for closing. The buyer's money clears the tax, any liens and your mortgage, and you get what is left. After that the deed is filed and the account passes to the new owner.

Gather your latest statement, Notice of Valuation and any protest papers before you call the title officer. Tell the buyer about a protest that is still open, because a change in value will land on them rather than you.

If you are unsure whether you ever claimed an exemption, call the Assessor and ask what is on file for the parcel. A missing exemption is easier to fix before a sale than after one. Ask the Treasury about service liens at the same time, so one round of phone calls covers every balance that could show up on the settlement statement, and you can plan your closing date around real numbers.

If you owe tax and want to sell

Start by finding the exact amount, since a delinquent balance gathers interest and may be sold as a tax lien. Treasury publishes a delinquent real property list and takes questions at propertytaxinfo@denvergov.org, where you should send your parcel ID, address and payment dates if a notice looks wrong.

  • Get the live balance in hand before listing or signing a contract.
  • Find out if earlier years are still open, not just the current one.
  • Look for service liens, which Treasury handles too.
  • Mention the debt to any buyer up front so closing can absorb it.

Cash deals can close quickly, with the tax paid from proceeds just like a mortgage payoff, which stops the account from slipping further while you decide. On a regular listing the title company requests the figure, prints it on the settlement statement and sends the money to Treasury when the deed records.

Frequently asked questions

What is the property tax protest deadline in Denver County?

June 8 each year. When June 8 falls on a weekend or holiday, the deadline moves to the next business day, and the Notice of Valuation explains how to file.

How often does Denver reappraise homes?

Once every two years, in odd-numbered years. The 2025 values drew on sales between July 1, 2022 and June 30, 2024.

Who sets the tax rate in Denver?

Taxing authorities set the mill levies in December. The Assessor neither sets rates nor collects money. The 2024 combined general levy in Denver was 79.202 mills.

When are Denver property taxes due?

Half payments are due the last day of February and June 15, and full payment is due April 30.

Can I sell a Denver house if the taxes are unpaid?

Yes. The balance comes out of your sale proceeds. Ask Treasury for the current amount first, so closing holds no surprises.

Boulder County property tax basics

Property tax here is split between two elected offices: the Assessor, who decides values, and the Treasurer, who mails bills and takes payments. The county covers about 740 square miles, with the City of Boulder as its seat, and neighbors Larimer, Weld, Broomfield, Jefferson, Gilpin and Grand counties. It had 330,758 residents in 2020 and an estimated 328,560 in July 2025.

Cities and towns inside it include Boulder, Longmont, Lafayette, Louisville, Erie, Lyons, Nederland, Superior, Jamestown and Ward. They all bill through the same Treasurer, so a house in Lyons and a house in Lafayette share due dates.

Homes are valued high. The median owner-occupied home is worth $756,300, and 62.0% of homes are owner-occupied. Roughly 38% are rented, which means many sellers are landlords who also carry license and inspection costs in places like Boulder. At these values, even small rate changes shift a bill by hundreds of dollars.

The yearly tax calendar

The Colorado tax year opens on the January 1 assessment date and closes with the levies set in December.

  • January 1: assessment date for all taxable property, and the day the general tax lien attaches.
  • By May 1: Notices of Valuation for real property go out.
  • By June 8: real property appeals are filed.
  • August 25: the Assessor sends the Abstract of Assessment to the state and tells the taxing entities their values.
  • By December 15: local entities certify their levies.
  • By December 22: county commissioners levy the taxes.

Boulder County's own appeals page adds an August 15 determination date and a September 15 Board of Equalization deadline.

Assessment rates and the bill

Each taxing body applies its own mill levy to the assessed value, and your bill adds those pieces together. Assessed value is actual value times the state's assessment rate.

Property type2025 rate2026 rate
Residential, school districts7.05%7.05%
Residential, local government6.25%6.8%

Agricultural, renewable energy27%25%
Oil and gas production87.5%87.5%

For 2026, the local government side first subtracts 10% of the first $700,000 of a home's actual value. School district math skips that step. The Treasurer's account lookup shows the real figure for any address.

Payment dates and interest

For 2026 the Treasurer listed March 2 and June 15 for half payments, or April 30 for the full amount. Send checks and money orders to the Boulder County Treasurer, and never mail cash.

A postmark sets the payment date. Interest on a first-half payment starts at 1% in March and reaches 6% by August. A full payment made in May costs 1% and reaches 4% by August. A second-half payment made June 16 to 30 costs 1% and reaches 3% in August.

For September through December, call the Treasurer. Payments after August 1 may carry extra fees.

Treasurer's offices

The main Treasurer office sits on the first floor at 1325 Pearl St. in Boulder and keeps weekday hours of 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. A Longmont office at 515 Coffman St., Suite 113, opens on Mondays only.

  • Phone: 303-441-3520
  • Email: treasurer@bouldercounty.gov
  • Mail: P.O. Box 471, Boulder, CO 80306
  • The Lafayette office at 1755 S. Public Road is closed until late January 2027.

Phone the office to confirm how online payment works before you count on it.

How to appeal your assessment

Real property appeals are accepted from May 1 through June 8, and a late filing forfeits the right to appeal. File by email, mail, fax, online, drop box or in person at 1325 Pearl St., second floor.

A well-built appeal names the value you think is right, explains where the Assessor's figure goes wrong, and lists comparable sales by address, price and date. For this cycle the sales window runs July 1, 2022 to June 30, 2024, and if few sales exist, verified sales from up to five years earlier can be used.

You can also correct record errors, such as square footage, bedroom and bath count, lot size or basement finish. The Assessor's phone is 303-441-3530 and its email is assessor@bouldercounty.gov.

Once the Notice of Determination arrives, you can appeal in writing to the county Board of Equalization until September 15. After the board mails its decision there are 30 days left to choose among the State Board of Assessment Appeals, district court and binding arbitration. Business personal property appeals are filed June 15 to June 30.

Selling with unpaid tax

Unpaid real property tax can be sold as a tax lien at the county's annual auction in November, and liens sold in 2026 carry 13% annual interest. The Treasurer posts the properties advertised for sale and updates the spreadsheet each Friday. Delinquent payments must be in certified funds.

To a seller, an unpaid balance is simply another closing item that the title company settles out of the sale. Colorado pays property tax in arrears, so a house sold in the spring may carry a bill for the prior year, and the January 1 lien date is why the closing agent checks the Treasurer's records.

Fire and flood history

On December 30, 2021 the Marshall Fire burned across 6,026 acres, destroying an estimated 1,084 structures and damaging 149. The September 2013 flood destroyed 262 homes in the county and damaged nearly 300. Anyone selling a house with that history should keep repair records, because buyer questions start there.

From accepted offer to payoff

Once you accept an offer, the title company opens the file and asks the Treasurer where the account stands. It wants to know which halves are paid, whether interest has been added and whether the parcel appears on the advertised lien list. If a balance exists, it is paid from your proceeds, and the settlement statement shows the amount.

Timing matters because interest is added monthly. A closing pushed from one month into the next can change the payoff, so ask for an updated figure when the date moves. If you appealed your value, tell the buyer, since a lowered value affects the next bill, and hand over the Notice of Determination.

A cash buyer fits this process easily: no lender is checking the tax account, and the sale can close once the payoff and the deed are in order. Houses with deferred repairs, flood history or tenants are the cases where an as-is sale tends to save the most time. Whichever route you choose, write down who you spoke with at the county and what figure they quoted, so that a later question about the payoff has a paper trail behind it.

Seller's to-do list

  • Before choosing a closing date, request a payoff from the Treasurer.
  • Read your valuation notice as soon as it arrives in May, because the appeal window lasts only about five weeks.
  • Keep the Notice of Determination if you appealed, as it shows the value of record.

Deed recording runs $43 per document in this county, and the state's documentary fee of one cent per $100 over $500 comes on top.

Frequently asked questions

What is the deadline to appeal a Boulder County valuation?

June 8 is the last day for real property, up to 11:59 p.m. Late filings are not accepted.

When are Boulder County property taxes due?

Half payments are due March 2 and June 15, or the full amount April 30.

Who sets my Boulder County property value?

The county Assessor does, working from sales between July 1, 2022 and June 30, 2024. Setting the tax rate is not part of the job.

Can I appeal my Boulder County tax bill itself?

No. Taxes are set by budgeting bodies such as county commissioners, city councils, school boards and special districts. You can appeal the value only.

How much interest applies if I pay late in Boulder County?

It depends on the month and the payment type. A full payment made in May carries 1%, while a first-half payment made in May carries 3%. For later months, call 303-441-3520.

Arapahoe County in brief

Arapahoe County is long and narrow, running from the southern Denver suburbs out to the eastern plains. Littleton is the county seat. It covers 805 square miles, stretching about 72 miles from east to west while measuring only 4 to 12 miles across. The 2020 census counted 655,070 residents, the third largest county population in Colorado.

Its cities and towns include Aurora, Centennial, Cherry Hills Village, Englewood, Greenwood Village, Littleton, Sheridan, Columbine Valley, Deer Trail, Foxfield and Glendale. Bennett, Bow Mar and Strasburg lie partly inside it. Nine public school districts serve the county, and your district shows up on your tax bill through its mill levy: Aurora, Bennett, Byers, Cherry Creek, Deer Trail, Englewood, Littleton, Sheridan and Strasburg.

Aurora and Centennial

Aurora, the biggest city, is split among three counties. Of its 386,261 residents in 2020, 336,035 lived in Arapahoe County, 47,720 in Adams and 2,506 in Douglas. A parcel's county decides who bills the tax, so an Aurora address alone tells you little.

Centennial is the other large city, with 108,418 residents in 2020. It was formed in 2001 from unincorporated Arapahoe County, including the former Castlewood and Southglenn areas. Most of it falls in Cherry Creek Public Schools, with the western part in Littleton Public Schools. Aurora is served by Aurora Public Schools and in places by Bennett and Brighton 27J. If your house is near a district line, school assignment can change from one block to the next, and buyers ask about it.

Homes near light rail stations or the interstate and E-470 corridors trade convenience for noise, and buyers price that in. A seller relocating for work or leaving after a layoff often needs a quick close.

Payment deadlines

Property owners here can pay one lump sum by April 30 or two installments, the first at the end of February and the second on June 15. The source is C.R.S. 39-10-104.5, a statewide rule that Arapahoe follows.

  • First installment: end of February.
  • Second installment: June 15.
  • Single payment: April 30, interest-free when on time.
  • Late interest: one percent each month, and any piece of a month is billed as a full month.
  • A total below $25 has to be paid whole by April 30.

A mailed payment counts as received on its postmark date. With no postmark, a payment that arrives within five days of the due date is credited to the due date. A deadline landing on a weekend or holiday rolls forward to the next business day. The Arapahoe County Treasurer can confirm any change.

How to appeal your valuation

Begin by telling the assessor you believe the value is too high. Use the form that came with your notice of valuation, or write a letter. State law lets you object if the property was valued too high, valued twice, or is exempt, and the assessor must consider whatever information you present. Check your notice of valuation for the exact filing date.

If the assessor leaves the value alone, the assessor owes you written reasons and two copies of the completed form by mail. A bare denial does not satisfy that requirement. The next stop is the county board of equalization.

Keep a copy of everything you file and note the day you filed. If a buyer is in the picture, mention the open appeal, because a lowered value changes later bills.

Tax left unpaid turns into a lien the county is allowed to sell. C.R.S. 39-11-101 obliges the treasurer to mail every owner of last year's unpaid tax a letter by September 1, stating the amount and a payment date at least fifteen days out.

You can still sell a house with taxes owing. What you owe in back tax, interest and fees is deducted from your sale money, so have the title company obtain an exact payoff from the treasurer. When an owner has died or is behind on several bills, a buyer who pays cash and closes on your timeline can keep a lien sale from becoming the deciding event.

How the sale and the tax bill meet at closing

The tax calendar and a sale rarely line up neatly, so the title company reconciles them for you. It looks up what has been paid, what is still owed and what interest has built, then settles any balance out of the money you would otherwise receive. You see the result as a line on the settlement statement.

Two details help you spot a mistake. First, whether you paid in two halves or all at once changes what is credited. Second, interest is figured by the month, so a payoff quote is only good through a stated date. If your closing slips into a new month, ask for a refreshed quote rather than assuming the old number still works.

What a cash sale skips is the lender's side of the process: the appraisal, the underwriting and the loan conditions that can hold up a closing. The tax payoff, the deed and the recording still happen the same way, so gather those documents early. Having the latest tax statement, any notice of valuation and your deed on hand also lets a buyer or title officer answer questions in one phone call instead of several.

Seller's checklist before closing

Start with the parcel: its county, school district and tax bill. Then note where today falls in the tax calendar.

  • Tell the title company whether you paid in two halves or in full, so the right amount is credited.
  • Keep every notice of valuation, and note the date of any objection you filed.
  • If a September notice from the treasurer arrived, treat its payment date as the real deadline.

June 15, under C.R.S. 39-10-104.5. February's last day is the first-half date, and April 30 is the date for paying everything at once.

Is all of Aurora in Arapahoe County?

No. The city crosses into Adams and Douglas counties too. In 2020, most of its residents, 336,035 of 386,261, lived on the Arapahoe side.

What interest applies if I pay late?

One percent monthly, rounding any part of a month up. For example, a first-half payment made in April carries 2 percent.

Can I sell my Arapahoe County house if I owe property tax?

Yes. At closing the title company normally pays the balance from your proceeds, using a payoff number it obtains from the treasurer.

What can I object to on my valuation notice?

State law lets you object if the property was valued too high, valued twice, or is exempt. If the assessor leaves the value alone, you are owed written reasons.

Eagle County at a glance

Eagle County is a mountain county in western Colorado with the Town of Eagle as its seat and Edwards as its largest community. The 2020 census counted 55,731 people, and the 2025 estimate is 54,291. Interstate 70 crosses the county east to west.

Much of the land is public. White River National Forest covers a large share and the Bureau of Land Management manages much of the rest, so check what your parcel borders before you list. Three school systems reach into the county: Eagle County School District RE-50J, Roaring Fork RE-1 and West Grand 1-JT, which is worth confirming for a buyer asking about a particular address.

How the Assessor values a home

The Eagle County Assessor values residential property by the market approach, using verified comparable sales as of a January 1 assessment date. The county reappraises in odd-numbered years, and the June 30, 2024 appraisal date applies to tax years 2025 and 2026. Sales data came from the 24 months ending June 30, 2024, or five years when data was thin.

Assessment rates have changed in the last few years:

  • 2024: 6.7% for residential, and 27.9% for vacant, commercial and industrial.
  • 2025: 7.05% for the school calculation and 6.25% for non-school, with other property at 27%.
  • 2026: 7.05% school and 6.8% non-school, with commercial improved and agricultural at 25% and all other at 26%.

For 2026 the non-school residential calculation also reduces actual value by 10% of the first $700,000. The school calculation uses the full value. If you own a second home and wonder whether that changes anything, ask the Assessor's office.

How the bill is calculated and why it rose

Assessed value times the combined mill levy gives the bill. About 90 taxing authorities set levies across roughly 367 taxing districts in the county. Bills for 2025 rose around 10% or more for many owners, because residential values climbed 8% under the reappraisal and a temporary $55,000 value reduction passed in 2024 expired.

The county average levy is about 65 mills, and some metro districts reach 125 mills, such as the Buckhorn area of Gypsum. The Tax Area code on your Notice of Valuation, in a format such as 236, P236 or SC236, tells you which authorities apply, and the county posts a spreadsheet of taxing authorities by area. Final amounts depend on the levies set in December, so confirm with the Treasurer in January.

Appealing your valuation

Notices are mailed May 1, and appeals can be filed from May 1 through June 8, postmarked or delivered by that date. Ways to file:

  • Online at appealeaglecounty.com, which the county prefers.
  • In person from 9:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m. if you can't file online.
  • By mail to Eagle County Assessor, P.O. Box 449, Eagle, CO 81631, or by fax at 970-328-8667.
  • An agent needs your written authorization, and you should keep proof of mailing.

Useful evidence includes an appraisal dated within six months before June 30, 2024, sales details on your property or comparables, or corrections to property details. A follow-up inspection may be needed.

The Assessor mails a Notice of Determination on or before June 30. If you disagree, or hear nothing, file a written appeal with the County Board of Equalization by July 15. The office phone is 970-328-8640, or toll free 800-225-6136.

Unpaid taxes and the lien sale

Real estate taxes still unpaid at the end of October are sold at the November tax lien sale, usually on the first or second Wednesday. The county's timeline:

  • May, June, August and September: calls or emails to delinquent owners when contact details are on file.
  • July 31: delinquent notice deadline. Payment by August 1 keeps a lien investor from adding current-year taxes to a prior lien.
  • October: unpaid real estate and mobile home taxes are published in the newspaper for three weeks.
  • November: the tax lien sale.

To redeem a sold lien, payment must reach the Treasurer by the last business day of the month, in cash or certified funds, from the owner of record. Seniors and active military can ask about deferral at colorado.propertytaxdeferral.com or (833) 634-2513.

Paying and getting a tax certificate

Call the Treasurer at 970-328-8860 for balances, and email taxcerts@eaglecounty.us to request a tax certificate. Payment options:

  • Card online.
  • Check payable to Eagle County Treasurer, mailed to PO Box 479, Eagle, CO 81631.
  • Wire. Call 970-328-8868 for instructions and verify them by phone, because the county warns of cyber fraud.

Bank bill pay can arrive late and unpostmarked, so interest may apply even when you paid on time. If a lender pays from escrow, the Treasurer cannot send duplicate statements to the mortgage company, since state law sends statements to the owner of record. Ask the office directly how a payoff works at closing.

What sellers in the Eagle valley run into

Common complications are large levies in some metro districts, reappraisal jumps and mortgage escrow shortfalls, and each can slow a conventional sale. Owners of inherited homes, out-of-area owners and landlords often want a clean exit with no showings. A cash purchase that accepts the house as it is, with tax and any lien paid from proceeds, fits that need.

Before you accept any offer, get the Treasurer's balance, confirm your Tax Area, and note whether a Board of Equalization appeal is still open, since a successful appeal lowers the next bill for whoever owns the house. At closing, the title company asks for the tax certificate, pays what is owed and records the deed.

A practical order for a seller: call the Treasurer for the balance, request the tax certificate by email, check which half has been paid, and confirm whether any late charge from the table above already applies. If a lien was sold at the November sale, remember that redemption needs cash or certified funds from the owner of record, so ask the title company to coordinate that payment rather than sending it yourself. Keep your Tax Area code and parcel details handy for every call, and save any email confirmations you receive about balances or certificates until the sale has closed and the deed has recorded, in case a question comes up later.

What is Eagle County's property valuation appeal window?

May 1 through June 8, postmarked or delivered by June 8. File online at appealeaglecounty.com or use the form on your Notice of Valuation.

When is the first half of Eagle County property tax due?

The last day of February. The second half is due June 15, and full payment is due April 30.

What is Eagle County's average mill levy?

About 65 mills on average, though some metro districts reach 125 mills.

Where do I send an Eagle County tax payment?

Eagle County Treasurer, PO Box 479, Eagle, CO 81631, with your tax coupon and account number.

What is the next step after the Assessor denies my appeal?

File a written appeal with the County Board of Equalization by July 15.

Assessor and Treasurer offices

Think of two desks. One decides what your house is worth, and that is the Assessor. The other mails the bill and takes your check, and that is the Treasurer, who then hands the money to the taxing districts. Neither desk sets your rate.

Lawmakers in Denver fix the assessment rate. Due dates and delinquency

You have a choice: split the bill or pay it once. Half is due at the end of February, the other half June 15, and anyone paying everything at once has until April 30. When a deadline falls on a weekend or legal holiday, the next business day counts.

  • September: the Treasurer advertises the unpaid real estate accounts.

  • October: the auction.

The tax lien sale

Unpaid real estate tax ends up at an October lien auction. Any account still carrying a balance in late October joins that year's sale. What an investor buys is the lien, so you keep the right to redeem it.

Ask for a payoff figure at (719) 520-7900. To redeem, your payment has to be in the Treasurer's hands by the last business day of the month. A lien nobody redeems can eventually lead to a treasurer's deed.

If you know about a lien, either pay it off or plan for the payoff at closing. The tax certificate from the Treasurer shows where the account stands today and any amount still owed.

How El Paso County values homes

Every odd-numbered year the state reappraises all real property, and a Notice of Valuation reaches El Paso County owners soon after May 1. Values from 2025 carry through tax year 2026, and they rest on a base year of 2023.

With 283,492 active real property parcels in 2023, mobile homes included, the office relies on mass appraisal. Houses must be valued by the market approach under state law, so a flat price per square foot is not allowed. Staff watch permits for new garages, decks, finished basements and additions, and they note demolitions and fires that cut value.

The sales that fed the 2025 and 2026 values ran from January 1, 2023 through June 30, 2024. Anything that sold later will not move your value until the next reappraisal.

You get a written Notice of Determination from the Assessor by August 15. Still unhappy? Take it to the County Board of Equalization at 1675 W. Garden of the Gods Road. Start any of them within 30 days of the Board of Equalization's decision letter. Arbitration results cannot be challenged.

Tax paperwork for selling a house

  • Anyone else can mail the request form with a $10 check payable to El Paso County Treasurer, Attn: Tax Certificates.
  • Allow 48 hours of processing once the office receives a mailed request.

Online search covers just the current billing cycle and can miss older balances or special assessments billed afterward, so order the certificate. When a signed certificate shows all taxes paid and all tax sales redeemed, it is conclusive proof the parcel was clear of property taxes on that date.

Prepaying next year's tax? It has to arrive by noon on the last business day of December. Later payments carry a January receipt date.

Selling with taxes owed

Owing tax does not stop a sale. Here is how it normally plays out.

  1. Your title company requests the Certificate of Taxes Due.
  2. It lists what is owed this cycle. A lien already sold? Phone (719) 520-7900 for the payoff.
  3. Closing pays the balance out of your proceeds.

Half is due the last day of February and half June 15, or the whole amount by April 30. Weekend and holiday dates roll to the next business day.

June 8 is the last day. The window opens May 1, right after notices go out, and the Assessor answers by August 15.

Delta County in brief

On Colorado's Western Slope, Delta County was split off from Gunnison County on February 11, 1883. A small house in Delta and an orchard property near Paonia will land far from it, and your tax bill follows your own property's assessed value. A house in the city, a farm lot near Hotchkiss and a place in Cedaredge can also sit in different tax areas with different mill levies, so the address matters more than the county name.

How Delta County calculates the bill

Delta County takes actual value, multiplies by an assessment rate, and then applies each taxing authority's mill levy for the tax area your property is in. In order:

  1. Use on January 1 decides how the Assessor classifies the property.
  2. Houses are valued from comparable sales alone, and the 2025 and 2026 tax years use sales from July 1, 2022 through June 30, 2024.
  3. Since 2025 houses carry two assessment rates, with schools on one and other local governments on the other. The county's own 2025 illustration shows 6.25 percent and 7.05 percent respectively.
  4. Every taxing authority sets its mill levy by dividing the revenue it needs by the assessed value within its boundary.

The money stays local and none of it pays for state services. Levies differ between tax areas, so your own bill is the only reliable number.

How to appeal a valuation

  • Explain why the number is wrong and name the value you think is right.

Earlier tax years are off the table in this process, and the Assessor can't weigh sales after June 30, 2024. Phone the Assessor to confirm dates before filing.

Offices and ways to pay

Value is the Assessor's job and billing is the Treasurer's. The Assessor works from 375 W. 6th St., Delta (970-874-2120) on weekdays, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., though hours are shorter during the protest season of May 1 through June 8.

Late tax collects one percent interest every month, and a partial month counts as a whole one (C.R.S. 39-10-104.5). The clock starts March 1 for a missed first half, June 16 for a missed second half and May 1 for a missed full payment.

There is a grace period on the first half. Pay within 30 days of the statement being mailed and no delinquent interest builds. After that the treasurer may sell the lien at the annual sale, leaving a buyer with a claim on the house that has to be cleared before you can sell cleanly.

Next, call the Treasurer to learn which halves are paid and whether any interest has started. Finally, give the title company your statement so it can request the tax certificate early.

At closing the Clerk and Recorder files the deed for $43. If you are tackling a sale from out of town, the phone numbers above cover all three offices, and the Treasurer accepts mailed payments, though only a USPS postmark counts as proof of timing.

Selling with tax due or a deferral

An outstanding balance doesn't block a sale. Back taxes, interest and any lien payoff are cleared at closing out of the price, so there is no cash to find beforehand. Before closing, the title company requests a tax certificate from the Treasurer, and the county runs an online portal for that request.

Any unpaid tax comes out of your proceeds, so the closing statement shows one payoff figure instead of several. Ask early which accounts the certificate covers, because each lien payoff adds a line to what the buyer's funds must clear.

A state property tax deferral is another matter. It is recorded as a junior lien. Repayment falls due 90 days after a sale or a contract of sale, and interest has been running since May 1 of the year it was claimed. When an owner dies and no spouse survives, repayment is due a year later.

A Delta County house that needs repairs, carries a tax lien or came through an estate can get a written cash offer from us in its current condition. Before you decide, dig out your latest statement, see whether the first half is paid and ask the title company if another lien sits ahead of the tax.

Frequently asked questions

When is Delta County property tax due?

Pay in full by April 30, or in two halves due the last day of February and June 15. Amounts of $25 or less must be paid in full by April 30.

What is the protest deadline for a Delta County property value?

Real property protests are due June 8, by mail, in person or by phone. An appeal to the County Board of Equalization follows by July 15.

What interest does Delta County charge on late property tax?

One percent per month under C.R.S. 39-10-104.5, with part of a month counted as a whole month. It starts March 1 for a late first half, June 16 for a late second half and May 1 for a late full payment.

Where do I pay property tax in Delta County?

Pay at the Treasurer's office at 501 Palmer Street, Suite 202, Delta, at the County Annex in Hotchkiss, by mail to PO Box 580, Grand Junction, or online through GovPros.

Does selling a house in Delta County end the property tax deferral?

A sale or contract of sale makes the state's deferral repayment due within 90 days. The deferral is a recorded junior lien, so it is paid at or soon after closing.

Hot Sulphur Springs is the county seat and Granby is the largest community. The county had 15,717 residents in 2020 and an estimate of 16,496 for 2025. Property tax offices in Jefferson County

Three things produce the amount: the Assessor's value and classification, assessment rates set by the General Assembly, and the mill levy each taxing entity sets.

Where Jefferson County sits

The county runs along the Front Range next to Denver and covers about 774 square miles. Golden is the seat and Lakewood is the biggest city, while mountain communities such as Conifer and Pine are unincorporated. The address of your house decides which city, fire district and school district levies appear on the notice.

Payment dates

Colorado property tax is paid in arrears, which means 2025 taxes were payable in 2026. The Treasurer mails notices in late January with coupons attached.

  • Last day of February: first half. If that date falls on a weekend, the county moves it to the next business day.
  • April 30: the whole year in one payment.
  • June 15: second half.

A U.S. postmark counts for the February, April and June deadlines. When the end of one of those months lands on a Friday or weekend, the county takes payment the next business day without delinquent interest. Online payments can take several days to leave your bank account, so start early.

When a tax bill goes unpaid

Unpaid real estate taxes are advertised in the fall and sold as a lien to an investor in November. Delinquent notices go out in July. In August, a tax buyer holding an older lien can pay the current year's tax, which adds to that certificate.

  • Early October: the first of three weekly newspaper notices for unpaid real property taxes. Advertising can begin in September, and paying before September 1 avoids the advertising charge.
  • November: the annual tax lien sale, run as an internet sale.
  • Redemption: the owner has three years to redeem by paying the delinquent tax plus accrued interest.
  • After three years: the certificate holder may apply for a public auction of a certificate of option for a treasurer's deed.

Redemption payments must reach the office by 5 p.m. on the last business day of the month, in cash or certified funds. Postmarks do not count, and interest accrues monthly. Call 303-271-8330 for a payoff figure.

How to appeal your valuation

File with the Assessor from May 1 through June 8. A mailed appeal must be postmarked by June 8, and the county suggests filing early since the last days get busy.

  1. Read the Notice of Valuation mailed May 1 and check the value and classification.
  2. Look up comparable sales in the Property Records Search, or call 303-271-8666 about inventory for up to three residences.
  3. File the appeal form, mail it, or book an appraiser appointment online.
  4. Watch for a Notice of Determination by August 15.
  5. If you still disagree, file with the Board of Equalization by September 15.
  6. The Board must finish hearings by November 1 and notify petitioners within five business days.
  7. A Board decision can be appealed within 30 days.

If a deadline is close, confirm the later dates with the Assessor before you rely on them.

The 2026 valuation cycle

The last reappraisal was in 2025, which makes 2026 an intervening year. Owners whose value did not change generally got no full notice, and postcard notices of value went only to owners with changes such as new construction.

Values for this cycle use a June 30, 2024 valuation date, and the Assessor looked only at sales from July 1, 2022 to June 30, 2024. If your house or a neighbor's sold higher or lower after that, the later sale will not show in the 2025 and 2026 values.

Taxes and liens when you sell

Taxes are paid in arrears, so a sale that closes in 2026 still leaves a 2026 bill that arrives in January 2027. Ask your title or escrow company how that bill will be split, and clear any past due balance first.

  • Ask the Treasurer about the prepayment cutoff: next year's taxes can be prepaid until noon on the last business day of December.
  • Check whether a Public Trustee release is needed for an old loan.
  • Use certified funds if you mail a payment to redeem a lien.

What to bring to the Treasurer or title company

Sellers get through the tax step faster with a few facts in hand. Have your parcel or account number ready, along with the notice you received in January and proof of any payment you made since. If you pay through a lender, ask for the date and amount of the last disbursement.

When a lien from an earlier year is on the account, phone 303-271-8330 and ask for the redemption figure and the date it is good through. Interest accrues monthly, so the number changes. If an older loan was paid off but the deed of trust is still on record, contact the Public Trustee at 303-271-8580 about the release before a buyer's title company asks.

Finally, keep a copy of the Assessor's Notice of Valuation. A buyer's agent may want to see what value the county has on the house, and the Assessor at 303-271-6511 can answer questions about classification.

Wildfire rules for mountain homes

The Wildfire Resiliency Code, approved March 10, 2026 and effective July 1, 2026, applies to unincorporated properties in the wildland urban interface. It reaches new construction and exterior alterations, re-roofing and re-siding included, and it is not retroactive.

A roof replacement of 25% or more must be a Class A assembly. A county approved Wildfire Mitigation Specialist must inspect defensible space. Re-siding projects that call for Zone 1 standards may use a self-attestation form.

For a seller in Conifer, Pine or the foothills, this can add cost to a repair list. Read the county's defensible space page before you hire a roofer.

Does a cash sale change the tax picture?

No. Whatever you owe the Treasurer, whether unpaid taxes, a lien or a mortgage balance, still gets settled at or before closing. A direct buyer's offer works best when you already know your payoff numbers, so collect them from the Treasurer, your lender and the Public Trustee before you answer.

Appeals to the Assessor are due by June 8, and mailed appeals must be postmarked that day. The window opens May 1 when notices of valuation go out.

Half is due the last day of February and half June 15, or the whole bill by April 30. Notices mail in late January.

Can I pay my Jefferson County taxes in installments?

Yes. Colorado allows two halves or one full payment. Ask the Treasurer at 303-271-8330 if you want to confirm your schedule.

How long do I have to redeem a Jefferson County tax lien?

The owner has three years to redeem by paying the delinquent taxes and accrued interest. Call 303-271-8330 for the payoff amount.

Call the Assessor at 303-271-6511. The Treasurer at 303-271-8330 can explain payments but cannot change a bill.

Adams County at a glance

Adams County lies north and east of Denver, and Brighton is the seat. It spans 1,184 square miles, nearly all land, and the South Platte River runs through it. The 2020 census counted 519,572 residents. Cities in the county include Arvada, Aurora, Brighton, Commerce City, Federal Heights, Northglenn, Thornton and Westminster, plus the towns of Bennett and Lochbuie.

Thornton is the biggest city here, and all of its 141,867 residents in 2020 lived on the Adams side. Commerce City had 62,418. Many of these cities spill over a county line, so a mailing address does not always tell you which treasurer bills the house. Aurora is the clearest case: 47,720 of its residents live in Adams County, and the rest are in other counties. A seller in the Adams slice of Aurora pays the Adams treasurer, while a neighbor a few blocks away may pay another county.

Four school districts serve Thornton, which covers Adams 12, Adams 14, Mapleton and Brighton 27J. Commerce City is served by Brighton 27J and Adams 14. District boundaries change the tax area, and the tax area changes the mill levy on your bill.

Commuting and what buyers notice

Interstates 25, 70, 76, 225 and 270 cross the county, along with several U.S. highways and the E-470 tollway. Quick access to Denver and the airport sells houses, though buyers also hear the highway noise when they tour. Thornton has three stops on the RTD N Line: Original Thornton/88th, Thornton Crossroads/104th and Eastlake/124th. A house a short drive from one of them is easier to market than a house that needs a long bus ride.

Adams County mixes dense suburbs with rural ground around Bennett, so a tract home in Thornton, a ranch parcel near Bennett and a bungalow in Commerce City face different cities, school districts and tax areas. Write down which ones apply to yours before you talk price.

Due dates

Adams County gives you two ways to pay. Split the bill into halves, or pay it all at once. Posted dates are February 28 for the first half, June 15 for the second, and April 30 for a lump-sum payment. The statute behind this, C.R.S. 39-10-104.5, ties the first half to the final day of February, which is why the date moves in a leap year.

The county takes half payments or full payments only, with nothing in between. If the whole bill is $25 or less, splitting is off the table and payment is due in one piece on the full-payment date. A U.S. postmark matching the due date counts as on time.

Colorado taxes are paid in arrears: what you pay in 2027 covers 2026. At a closing, the title company still splits the current year's tax between seller and buyer, even though that bill has not been written.

The treasurer's year runs in order. January brings tax notices. July brings delinquent notices. September brings a newspaper listing of unpaid real property. Late December is when the commissioners certify the tax roll and set the mill levy.

Late interest and small-balance charges

Late interest is one percent for each whole month, and the county posts a table with the running total. The second half begins at 1 percent for June 16 to 30 and climbs to 6 percent by November.

On small delinquencies, a treasurer may add an administrative charge of up to $25 where the delinquent tax totals under $50, with the combined figure held to $50. Penalty and interest amounts of $50 or less may be waived outright.

How to appeal your assessment

An appeal challenges the value of the property. It cannot lower a tax rate, because mill levies differ by tax area. Adams County takes filings from May 1 through June 8, by mail, email, fax or in person.

The owner has the standing to appeal. An attorney or anyone else acting for the owner must file a notarized letter of agency with the first appeal. Without it, the assessor will not take the case, and the owner waits for next year and files an abatement.

  • Notices of Value arrive by May 1.
  • You can appeal from May 1 to June 8.
  • Notices of Determination are mailed by August 15.
  • To dispute the determination, mail the completed form to the County Board of Equalization, due September 15.
  • The board hears cases from September 1 through November 1 and mails decisions within five days.
  • Once the board decides, 30 days remain to take the matter to the Board of Assessment Appeals, to district court in Brighton, or to binding arbitration.

Actual value rests on an appraisal as of June 30 of each even-numbered year, built from 24 months of sales data. Reappraisal of real property happens on a two-year cycle, so ask the assessor where your notice falls.

Selling with taxes owed

Taxes you do not pay eventually go to an online tax lien sale, which the county runs for about a month each fall. Before that, the treasurer mails delinquent notices in July and advertises unpaid real property in September. Paying before the end of October keeps your parcel out of it.

By September 1 the treasurer must also mail each owner who owes last year's tax a notice naming a payment date at least fifteen days away. Take that letter seriously: its date is the real cutoff.

You can still sell. At closing, the title company pays what you owe out of the sale money after getting a payoff quote from the treasurer. The Treasurer works from the Adams County Government Center, 4430 South Adams County Parkway, Brighton, and answers at 303-659-2120.

With a cash buyer there is no lender approval step, so closing can happen quickly when a lien sale is near. Confirm the payoff figure with the treasurer first so the closing statement is right.

What to gather before you list

Collect these items before you list, because buyers and the title company tend to ask for them early.

  • Your latest tax statement and proof of which half payments you made.
  • The Notice of Value and, if you appealed, the Notice of Determination.
  • Your tax area and school district, since both affect the bill.
  • A payoff quote from the treasurer if anything is delinquent.

Also write down the contact details for the treasurer and the assessor so you can reach them quickly when a question comes up in escrow. A buyer who closes with cash can skip the lender's appraisal and underwriting steps, and an as-is purchase means you do not have to fix deferred work to get to closing.

Frequently asked questions

June 15. The first half falls on the last day of February and a full payment on April 30. A postmark dated the due date is on time.

Can I pay part of my Adams County tax bill?

No. The county accepts half payments or full payments only. A total of $25 or less has to be paid in one payment by the full-payment date.

What is the deadline to appeal an Adams County valuation?

The assessor accepts appeals from May 1 to June 8. If you disagree with the determination, put your appeal to the county Board of Equalization in writing by September 15.

Where is the Adams County Treasurer?

At the Adams County Government Center, 4430 South Adams County Parkway, Brighton, CO 80601. The phone number is 303-659-2120.

What if I owe back taxes and want to sell my Adams County house?

You can still sell. The title company settles unpaid tax, interest and fees from your proceeds, working from a payoff the treasurer provides.

Broomfield County at a glance

Squeezed between Denver and Boulder, Broomfield is the state's smallest and youngest county, created on November 15, 2001. Population stood at 74,112 in 2020. A lot of its houses went up during the 1990s tech boom, which means roofs, water heaters and windows are now what buyers poke at.

City and county are a single government here. One office family sends your tax bill, files your deed and hears your valuation complaint, so a sale rarely sends you to a second courthouse. The address to know is One DesCombes Drive.

Due dates and penalties

Pick one of two schedules: a single payment in April, or two installments. Pay on time and no interest is added.

Paying by card online adds a 2.50% provider fee, and eCheck adds $2.50. A single online transaction tops out at $1,000,000. A bill under $25 has to go in as one full-year payment. For mailed checks, have the postal clerk hand-stamp the envelope.

Lateness costs more each month. A first-half payment that arrives in March carries 1%, and one that arrives in April carries 2%, which works out to 1% interest for every month past the due date.

The county mails the notice to whoever owns the property on record, never to your lender. If your mortgage includes escrow, confirm with the lender that it is sending the payment. Billing questions: 303-464-5810 or treasurer@broomfield.org.

How Broomfield values your home

Two offices split the work. The Assessor decides what your house is worth, and the Treasurer takes the money. Neither picks the rate, which comes from each school, fire and other district's own mill levy.

Values are reset every other year, in odd-numbered years, as of January 1. The model draws on two years of sales, and the 2025 round used July 1, 2022 through June 30, 2024. Between reappraisals your number holds unless something physical changes, such as new construction, a basement finish, an addition or a teardown.

Houses are priced by comparing them with recent sales of similar homes, and the Assessor posts sales lists for single family homes and condos. To talk to someone, use assessor@broomfield.org or 303-464-5819.

How to appeal your assessment

Real property owners can protest to the Assessor from May 1 through June 8. Filing options:

  • The online appeal portal, which includes a sales map of your neighborhood and lets you upload documents.
  • Mail it to Broomfield County Assessor, PO Box 1149, Broomfield, CO 80038-1149, with a June 8 postmark at the latest.
  • Walk it into the Community Assistance Center, in the lobby of the George Di Ciero City and County Building.

Bring what proves your case: an appraisal from inside the sales window, photos of damage or wear, similar homes that sold for less, and anything showing the county's record of your house is wrong. You get a Notice of Determination by June 30.

Still unhappy? File with the Board of Equalization by July 15. An independent hearing officer runs the hearing over Google Meet. Choose as many as five comparable sales in the online form, submit any new evidence at least three days ahead, and expect no rescheduling. Reach the clerk at clk-boe@broomfield.org or 303-438-6332, option 9.

Selling soon? Weigh the effort of an appeal against your closing date, since a lower value only helps the buyer's future bills once you no longer own the house.

Unpaid tax and the lien sale

Taxes that stay unpaid get sold as liens at a public sale, normally in November in the City Council Chamber. Delinquent accounts are advertised in a list that runs three weeks in a row before the sale.

A bidder buys the debt, not your house. You keep ownership through a three year redemption window on most properties, and few liens ever turn into a deed. Recent certificates paid thirteen percent. Anything nobody bids on stays with the county.

Bidders can bid premiums over the amount owed. Nobody refunds a premium when the lien is redeemed.

Selling with taxes owed

You don't need to be current to sell. Back tax comes out of your proceeds and the lien is released at the closing table. The usual sequence:

  1. Title orders a Certificate of Taxes Due (C.R.S. 39-10-115) from the Treasurer, showing everything paid apart from amounts listed as still owing.
  2. Whatever is owed becomes a payoff line on your settlement statement. Should a tax be missing from the certificate, Broomfield says it takes care of the omitted amount.
  3. Sell mid-year and you and the buyer divide that year's bill by days of ownership. Ask the title officer for line items before closing day.
  4. The deed gets recorded and the payoff goes to the county.

Before you list, pull your latest tax notice and any escrow statement so you know whether the current half is paid. If you have an open protest or a tax lien sale notice, tell the title officer at the start, since either can change what needs to be settled and when.

Owners living out of state face one extra rule. Colorado generally has the closing agent hold back the lesser of 2% of the price or the net proceeds, remitted on form DR 1079. If that overshoots what you owe, a Colorado return gets the difference back. The Department of Revenue guidance explains the form.

Recording a deed in Broomfield

Recording is handled at One DesCombes Drive on weekdays, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., closed on holidays. Call 303-464-5109 or write RecordingInformation@broomfield.org. Terms:

  • The fee is $40 regardless of page count, with a $3 surcharge on each document, in effect since July 1, 2025.
  • Leave an inch of margin top and bottom and half an inch on each side.
  • Drop-off and mail submissions need a cover sheet with your contact details, plus payment.
  • Most documents can go through the self service e-recording portal.

Anything filed since November 2001 is searchable online. Earlier documents sit in Adams, Boulder, Jefferson or Weld County, where the land used to belong. At a typical closing your title company does the recording.

What sellers in Broomfield run into

Trouble tends to come from three places: tax status, old records and the condition of the house. Hail beats up roofs first, and since the Marshall Fire of December 30, 2021 buyers and insurers look harder at fire risk. Find out what your insurer wants early.

Tired of repairs and open houses? A cash sale as-is skips listing prep, financing contingencies and appraisal waits. We purchase Broomfield County houses in their current shape and can handle tax balances, inherited title and tenant situations.

Frequently asked questions

When is Broomfield County property tax due?

Pay all at once by April 30, or split it into February 28 and June 15 installments. Meet those dates and there is no interest.

Who do I call about a Broomfield County property tax bill?

Billing goes to the Treasurer at 303-464-5810 or treasurer@broomfield.org. For value disputes, call the Assessor at 303-464-5819.

What is the deadline to protest a Broomfield County valuation?

Protests on real property are accepted May 1 to June 8, and mail needs a June 8 postmark. If the Assessor's answer doesn't satisfy you, the Board of Equalization deadline is July 15.

Can I sell a Broomfield County house with unpaid property tax?

Yes. The title company deducts what you owe from your proceeds and clears the lien at closing. If you do nothing, the debt can be sold at the November lien sale.

Does Broomfield County have a separate county recorder?

Not separately. The consolidated city and county runs its own Recording Division at One DesCombes Drive. Since July 1, 2025 the charge is $40 plus a $3 surcharge on each document.

Weld County and its tax base

North of Denver, Weld County spreads over 4,017 square miles and is governed from Greeley. Population was 328,981 in 2020 and is estimated at 378,426 for 2025. Farmland, oil and gas wells and busy suburbs all land on the same tax roll, and the appeal calendar reflects that: one deadline serves real property, and the same date applies to personal property, oil and gas, and producing mines.

Cities such as Greeley, Evans, Fort Lupton and Dacono sit in the county, along with towns such as Windsor, Johnstown, Firestone, Frederick, Mead and Severance. Windsor, Johnstown and Erie reach into adjoining counties, which means a house there could be billed by Weld or by the neighbor.

Which Weld County offices handle property tax

Property tax passes through three hands. One office sets the value, another hears disputes about it, and a third sends the bill and takes the money. The Assessor and the Treasurer and Public Trustee office share an address, 1400 N 17th Avenue in Greeley.

  • The Assessor prepares the roll and sets values. Email assessor@weld.gov or call (970) 353-3845.
  • The County Board of Equalization takes appeals once a Notice of Determination is issued: weld-cboe@weld.gov, (970) 400-3650.
  • The Treasurer mails notices, collects payments and runs the lien sale: PO Box 458, Greeley, CO 80632-0458, (970) 400-3290.
  • The Clerk and Recorder files the deed that changes who the owner of record is: 1250 H Street, Greeley, (970) 304-6530.

The Treasurer's notices are mailed before January ends, addressed to whoever the roll shows as owner.

Due dates and late interest

A Weld County bill is for the year just ended, due as of January 1. Three payment dates are posted: February 28 for the first half, June 15 for the second, and April 30 if you pay everything at once.

The two halves must be equal, and the county turns down partial payments. For a tax of $25.00 or less there is no splitting at all, so the entire amount is owed by the full payment date. Mail bearing a U.S. postmark on or before a deadline counts as on time.

Ways to pay

There are four ways to pay: mail, the web, a counter visit or the drop box.

  • By mail, enclose the payment coupon for each property and make a check, money order or cashier's check out to Weld County Treasurer. The address is PO Box 458, Greeley, CO 80632-0458.
  • On weldtax.com, an electronic check costs nothing. Debit and credit cards add a third-party fee.
  • At 1400 N 17th Avenue in Greeley, staff accept cash, checks, money orders, cashier's checks and cards. A Visa debit card carries a flat $4.00 charge.
  • The drop box, located north of the main building entrance, is for checks only. Cash and lien payments stay out of it.

When you and your lender both send money, the Treasurer keeps the lender's payment and returns yours. Lenders do not receive your notice from the county, so an escrow customer who wants the lender to see it should send a photocopy.

How to appeal your valuation

Disputes begin with a protest filed with the Assessor. An owner who is still unhappy can go to the County Board of Equalization, which is the Board of Commissioners acting under C.R.S. 39-8-101. Its review is limited to value. The tax amount itself is outside its reach.

Values on 2025 and 2026 bills come from market conditions on June 30, 2024, a date fixed by law. The Board looks only at sales and market data from 2023 and the first half of 2024, which rules out a purchase or appraisal made after June 30, 2024.

Real property shares a deadline with personal property, oil and gas, and producing mines. In 2026 it was September 15, received or postmarked, and the Board of Equalization page posts the date each year. Put the appeal in writing, then send it online, by mail, by fax to (970) 304-6433, by email or in person. A phone call does not count.

Only the owner may appeal. A person filing on the owner's behalf needs a signed letter of agency, and a late appeal is never heard.

What happens to the tax bill when you sell

An unpaid bill stays with the parcel, which is why it gets cleared at or before closing, normally by the title company. Because Colorado collects in arrears, the seller generally owes for the months they held the house, and the settlement statement shows how the title company divided the year.

A Certificate of Taxes Due, requested on a Treasurer form, is how title companies verify what is owed. Order it early when taxes are behind, since the interest chart keeps rising month after month.

A new owner's name gets onto the roll only through the recorded deed, after which the Assessor makes the change. If a notice never shows up, C.R.S. 39-10-103 still treats the tax as owed.

If Weld County taxes go unpaid

Every month of delay adds interest. Once a lien exists, payment has to be made at the Treasurer's office and processed by the month's last business day, since neither postmarks nor drop box items count.

Timing is the whole story for an owner who has fallen behind. The balance grows monthly, and a sale lets the closing agent pay what is owed out of the proceeds. We purchase Weld County houses as is and can respond to a house with back taxes in writing. Having the latest notice and a payoff figure from the Treasurer in hand speeds things up.

Programs that reduce the bill

Pages on the Treasurer's site cover senior programs, tax deferral and special assessments, and the Board of Equalization links to Senior Property Tax Exemptions. Look them over before listing. A deferral or exemption on your account can change what has to be paid at closing.

Steps for a seller with a Weld County bill

Sequence helps when you sell. Locate your latest notice and note which installments are paid. Have the title company request the certificate. Check that the county has your current mailing address. If a mortgage exists, find out whether the servicer pays your tax from escrow. After closing, confirm the deed was recorded, because that is what moves the new owner's name onto the roll. Little effort goes into any of this, and it heads off most tax surprises at the settlement table.

Frequently asked questions

When are property taxes due in Weld County, Colorado?

Taxes are due January 1 for the previous year. The county lists February 28 for the first half, June 15 for the second half and April 30 for full payment.

What is the Weld County property tax appeal deadline?

The Board of Equalization's deadline for real property appeals was September 15 in 2026, received or postmarked, and it posts the date each year. Late appeals are not considered.

Can I pay half of my Weld County property tax?

Yes, in two equal installments, unless the tax is $25.00 or less. The county does not accept partial payments.

Do I get a Weld County tax notice if my mortgage company pays my taxes?

Yes. The Treasurer mails the notice to the owner of record, and mortgage companies do not receive a copy from the county.

How do I get a Certificate of Taxes Due in Weld County?

Use the request form on the Treasurer's tax information page. Title companies commonly request it before closing.

Archuleta County in brief

Archuleta County is a mountain county in southwest Colorado, on the New Mexico line. Pagosa Springs is the seat, its largest town and its only incorporated municipality, so there is just one town government to deal with. The county covers 1,356 square miles, and 13,359 people lived there in the 2020 census, up from 9,898 in 2000. The 2025 estimate is 14,306. Public schools are run by Archuleta County School District 50-JT.

About 65 percent of the land is San Juan National Forest, the Weminuche and South San Juan wilderness areas, or Southern Ute reservation land. That leaves a limited supply of private building land. Pagosa Springs itself had 1,571 residents in 2020 and 964 housing units, and 33.9 percent of those were vacant at the census.

Some downtown buildings are heated with geothermal water. If your property uses geothermal heat, or a private well and septic system, say so up front, because buyers in a mountain county ask about utilities early.

River flooding and selling

The San Juan River runs through the middle of Pagosa Springs and has flooded the town more than once. A 1911 flood took out the water pipeline and every bridge in the county. On October 11, 2025, heavy rain pushed the river over its banks again, damaged several bridges and a sewer line, and closed part of U.S. Highway 160, the main road through town. Residents of Hermosa Street, San Juan Street and areas east of Hot Springs Boulevard were evacuated.

A house in or near the river corridor may draw flood questions from buyers, lenders and insurers. A buyer paying cash is not waiting on any of those sign-offs. If your property was damaged, keep photos, repair receipts and any insurance claim records. Whoever buys will use them to size up the work still needed.

Payment schedule

Archuleta County bills follow the statewide schedule. Owners may send the first half by the last day of February and the second by June 15, or settle the whole bill on April 30. That choice comes from C.R.S. 39-10-104.5. Anything paid late is charged one percent for each month, and a fraction of a month is billed as a whole month.

The Treasurer's office mails tax notices at the end of January each year. If yours has not shown up by mid-February, call. Owners can preview and pay online through the treasurer's portal, and can request e-statements with the Address Change and E-Notice Form.

A payment that has no postmark but arrives inside five days of the due date gets credited to the due date. When the total is less than $25, the whole amount is owed by April 30.

Assessor and Treasurer contacts

Value comes from the Assessor and collection from the Treasurer. Neither office decides the tax amounts, and the Assessor levies nothing. The Treasurer is an elected post with a four-year term.

Both offices are at 305 Village Drive in Pagosa Springs and are open Monday through Thursday, 7:00 am to 5:00 pm. Phone the Treasurer at 970-264-8325 and the Assessor at 970-264-8310. Mail goes to P.O. Box 790 for the Treasurer and P.O. Box 1089 for the Assessor, both in Pagosa Springs, CO 81147.

The Assessor posts these assessment rates:

  • Residential: 6.95% of market value
  • Multi-family: 6.80%
  • Vacant land: 29%
  • Agricultural: 26.40%
  • Lodging: 26.40%
  • Commercial and personal property: 29% of actual value

By May 1 each year the assessor must send out a notice of valuation. In even-numbered years, the value is printed on the tax bill instead.

The tax lien sale and redemption

If tax goes unpaid, the county may sell the lien to an investor, and the owner still has the right to redeem. The sale runs each autumn: research and bidding open in early October and close in early November, and winning bidders make a 10 percent deposit by ACH shortly before it closes.

  • Certificates from the current year's sale earn 13 percent.
  • Redeemed certificates earn 4.5 percent over the Federal Reserve Discount Rate as of September 2.
  • Most properties are redeemed.
  • Within three years of the sale, a buyer holding an unredeemed lien can apply for a Treasurer's Deed.
  • Liens expire and are cancelled after seven years.
  • If the owner has not paid the following year's tax by July 1, the buyer is notified and may pay it, and that amount is added to the lien.

All that added interest is why an owner with a delinquent house should act early. State law also requires the treasurer to mail a delinquency notice by September 1, with at least fifteen days to pay.

Selling with taxes due

Yes, you can sell. The title company takes the unpaid tax and interest out of the sale money, after requesting the amount from the Treasurer. Selling before a lien sale, or before a Treasurer's Deed application, lets you end the problem on your own terms.

Before you pick a closing date, call 970-264-8325 and get the Treasurer's payoff. Much of the county is public land, so private houses are a small share of what exists. Selling as-is to a cash buyer lets you leave deferred repairs undone.

Gather your latest tax statement, any lien paperwork and your notice of valuation before you list, so the title company can turn around a payoff fast.
