From offer to closing with a tax balance

If back tax is part of your situation, the sale usually moves in five steps. First, you accept an offer and the title company opens an order. Second, the title company obtains the Treasurer's payoff covering tax, interest and any lien charges. Third, a closing date is set, and the payoff is refreshed if the date slips, since interest grows monthly. Fourth, you sign the deed and the settlement statement. Fifth, the payoff is sent from your proceeds, the deed is recorded and the balance comes to you.

A cash sale shortens the middle of this sequence, because nothing depends on a lender's appraisal or approval. That matters most when a lien sale or a Treasurer's Deed application is on the calendar. Once a certificate has been sold, find out from the Treasurer how redemption works before closing, because redeeming is what clears the lien.

Notices to keep

Save the notice of valuation the Assessor mails each May, every tax statement, and any delinquency letter from the Treasurer. Together they show the value of record, what you have paid and what is still owed. A buyer or a title officer will ask for them, and having them ready shortens the back and forth.

Frequently asked questions

When is the first half of Archuleta County property tax due?

Under C.R.S. 39-10-104.5 it is due at the end of February. After that come June 15 for the second half and April 30 for a lump sum.

Where is the Archuleta County Treasurer?

305 Village Drive, Pagosa Springs, CO 81147. Doors are open Monday through Thursday from 7:00 am until 5:00 pm, and staff answer 970-264-8325.

What is the residential assessment rate in Archuleta County?

Residential property is assessed at 6.95 percent of market value.

How long before a Treasurer's Deed can be applied for?

Three years after the sale at most, and only if the lien is still unredeemed.

Can I sell if the house flooded?

Yes. Cash buyers take the house as it is, so repairs can wait. Hold on to repair records and insurance paperwork to show them.

Pueblo County in brief

The city of Pueblo is the seat and the biggest community here. In 2020 the county held 168,162 people, and about 86.9% of them lived in urban areas, which puts most owners inside city limits or close by. Pueblo School District 60 reaches nearly every address in the city, and Pueblo County School District 70 reaches only a few small pockets. A farm lot east of town, a house by the lake and a bungalow downtown fall under different taxing districts, so read the levies on your own statement.

Assessor and Treasurer offices

Value and classification belong to the Assessor, while billing and collecting belong to the Treasurer. You will find both inside the Pueblo County Historical Courthouse, 215 W. 10th Street, Pueblo, CO 81003.

Before a buyer asks, look up your parcel in the Assessor's property search and confirm the ownership, legal description and lot size. Mobile and manufactured homes are taxed as well, and moving permits for them come from the Treasurer.

Look for the Treasurer on the first floor, where the doors are open 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. on weekdays except holidays. Since the Assessor never sends a bill, any question about an amount due belongs there.

Protests and appeals

Disputes run in two stages. You protest to the Assessor first, and if that fails you take the case to the County Board of Equalization (CBOE). The county revalues real property every odd-numbered year and mails Notices of Valuation by May 1.

  • June 8 is the cutoff for a protest sent by mail (postmarked), made in person or sent by email, and nobody can protest once it is gone.
  • State your own value as of June 30, 2024, and add papers that back up a change.
  • A Notice of Determination follows from the Assessor on or before the last working day in June.
  • Want to keep going? A written appeal to the CBOE is due by July 15 under C.R.S. 39-8-106.

The dates on your own notice govern your case, so read them closely. A CBOE hearing lasts 20 minutes, shared between you and the Assessor, and once it is on the calendar it stays there.

One payment by April 30 settles the whole bill. If you prefer halves, send the first by the last day of February and the second by June 15. A bill of $25 or less must be paid in full by April 30.

Residential assessment rates for 2026 stand at 6.8% for local governments and 7.05% for schools. Multiply the assessed value by the combined mill levies of every district on your parcel and you have the bill.

If an old bill is still open, act before it grows. Tax left unpaid can end up in a lien sale run by the Treasurer's Redemption Department, and the bidding rules and fees for Treasurer's Deed auctions have changed. Owners who fall behind have some help. Volunteers in the Property Tax Work Off Program earn a voucher toward the January payment, and older residents can use the deferral program.

Selling with back taxes

Closing normally settles the tax for the year of sale. To get the figure, your title company requests a tax certification, which the Tax Certification Department issues to title companies and lenders.

  • Request the certification early, so a delinquency surfaces well ahead of the closing date.
  • Money still owed comes out of the sale proceeds, which means a lien need not kill the deal.
  • The county records the deed, and a transfer deed over $500 carries the state documentary fee of $.01 per $100.

A big tax bill on a house that needs work is where an as is cash sale can help, because nobody is waiting on a lender's appraisal. Send us your Pueblo County tax figures and we will go through them with you before you decide anything.

Preparing a protest

Documents carry a protest. Begin with your own estimate of value as of June 30, 2024, the date current values are measured against. Then back it up with whatever shows the house is worth less than the notice claims, such as a recent appraisal, photos of damage or deferred repairs, or sales of similar homes nearby.

The Assessor's property search also shows the lot size, legal description and ownership record on file. An error in square footage or lot size is easy to correct and better caught before a buyer's agent notices. Missing the deadline forfeits the protest for that year, so put June 8 on the calendar the day the May notice arrives.

How a sale moves through the Treasurer's office

Your title company does most of the tax legwork out of sight. If you know the sequence, you will notice when something stalls.

A deferral under the elderly program turns up here too, so expect the title company to ask for a payoff if you used one.

What a cash sale skips

Without a lender, a cash buyer has no appraisal to wait for and no list of required repairs. Taxes work the same way as in any sale: the certification still gets ordered, delinquent tax still comes out of proceeds, and the deed still gets recorded. You simply travel a shorter road when the house needs work and the bill is big.

Plan for a few days of back and forth between the title company and the Treasurer's staff, and keep copies of every certification and payment receipt. Those papers settle any later question about whether a year was paid.

Keep the calls straight. For value, lot records and ownership, dial the Assessor at 719-583-6597. For the bill, a payment or a lien, dial the Treasurer.

Help for older homeowners

If you have fallen behind, two programs are worth a look. The Redemption Department runs the tax deferral program for older residents, and the Property Tax Work Off Program turns volunteer hours into a voucher toward the January payment. Mesa County for homeowners

Mesa County sits on Colorado's Western Slope along the Utah line. Grand Junction is the seat and largest city, and the 2020 census counted 155,703 residents. Towns include Fruita, Palisade, Clifton, De Beque and Collbran, plus areas such as Redlands and Orchard Mesa. An owner here may hold a city lot, an orchard parcel or ground next to public land, and all of it is taxed under one county system.

The Treasurer and Assessor

The Assessor values property and hears protests. The Treasurer bills, collects and distributes the money. The Treasurer's office is in the Old Courthouse, 544 Rood Avenue, Grand Junction, CO 81501, open Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. The phone is 970-244-1824, and the mailing address is Dept 5027, P.O. Box 20,000, Grand Junction, CO 81502-5001.

The Treasurer's services include tax sale information, the Treasurer's deed, a senior and veteran exemption, and buying and selling a manufactured home.

The county also runs a Property Tax Deferral Program. An owner can postpone payment, and a lien is recorded on the property in exchange. A buyer's title company will see a recorded deferral lien, so it must be cleared when you sell.

Assessment and payment calendar

The statutory calendar starts January 1, the date all taxable property is listed and valued. These are the dates a home seller is most likely to need.

Appealing after the Assessor

If the Notice of Determination leaves you unhappy, mail a copy of the completed form to the Mesa County Board of Equalization by July 15 at P.O. Box 20000-5007, Grand Junction, CO 81502. You will then get a hearing date, and hearings run July 1 through August 5.

After a Board decision, the owner has 30 days from the postmark to go to one of three places: the Board of Assessment Appeals in Denver, Mesa County District Court at 125 N Spruce Street, or binding arbitration.

  • The Assessor reviews value and classification only, not the amount of tax.
  • Only the owner can file. An agent needs a notarized letter of agency.
  • Look up nearby sales in the county's database before you file.
  • Commercial rent producing property must attach two years of income, expense and rent roll data.

Values between reappraisals

Real property is reappraised every odd-numbered year, and that value generally carries into the even-numbered year after it. The appraisal date is June 30 of the year before the reappraisal year, and the county uses an 18 month stretch of sales ending that day.

That means a house sold after the sales window will not change your value until the next reappraisal, and a buyer may ask what the county has on file. Houses are valued by the market approach. Other property is valued with market, cost and income approaches.

The annual tax lien sale

Mesa County runs its tax lien sale as an online auction in early November through Real Auction. Bidders register ahead of time and put down a deposit of 10% of expected spending, and winning bids are due a few days after the sale.

An investor buys the lien, not the property, and a deed has followed in less than one percent of purchases. Redemption can happen any time until a Treasurer's deed issues. The yield is set at nine points above the federal discount rate as of September 1.

After August 1, certificate holders get first option to pay later years' unpaid taxes and endorse them on the certificate. That means a lien can grow if the next year's bill is missed too. Owners who expect to sell soon should keep every year current, so the payoff at closing is one year's balance and not several.

Paying the bill

The Treasurer mails the statement by January 31. You can send the whole amount by April 30, or split it into a February 28 payment and a June 15 payment. Owners who pay through a mortgage escrow account should still glance at the statement, since the county bill is what a buyer's title company will read.

The Treasurer's page also covers a senior and veteran exemption. If you hold one and are selling, tell your title company, because the closing figures should reflect what you actually owe.

Protesting your value: the first step

The Notice of Valuation comes with an appeal form. Fill it in and file it with the Assessor by June 8. The Assessor reviews value and classification only, so a protest about the size of the bill itself will go nowhere. Nearby sales in the county's database are the best evidence for a house.

Notices of Determination are mailed June 30. If the answer is no, the Board of Equalization is the next level, and the deadline to take it there is July 15. Only the owner can file, so if someone else handles your affairs, they need a notarized letter of agency.

A seller's timeline

Tax questions tend to surface at the same points in a Mesa County sale.

  • Before listing: check for a deferral lien, a prior year balance and the manufactured home title if one applies.
  • When you accept an offer: your title company reviews the account and asks for payoffs.
  • Before closing: confirm the figures with the Treasurer, because interest and any later-year payments by a lien holder can change the total.
  • At closing: liens and unpaid taxes are paid from your proceeds.

If you got a Notice of Valuation this spring and disagree with it, the protest window is separate from the sale. Mention an open protest to your agent so a buyer is not surprised by a later change in value.

Selling a Mesa County house with liens or back taxes

Look at deferral liens, unpaid prior year taxes and any manufactured home title questions before you list. The same payoffs apply whether the buyer uses a loan or cash. A direct buyer can close without a lender's appraisal conditions, but a lien is still paid at closing.

  1. Ask the Treasurer at 970-244-1824 where your account stands.
  2. Get a payoff for any deferral or delinquent balance.
  3. Have your title company confirm the lien is cleared in the closing figures.
  4. If the home is a manufactured home, check how the title is handled through the Treasurer's buying and selling process.

Frequently asked questions

When is the Mesa County property tax protest deadline?

The deadline to file a real property protest with the Assessor is June 8, after the Notices of Valuation go out by May 1. A weekend or holiday moves it to the next business day.

Where do I pay Mesa County property taxes in person?

The Treasurer is at the Old Courthouse, 544 Rood Avenue in Grand Junction, Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. The phone number is 970-244-1824.

Is the Mesa County tax lien sale online?

Yes. The sale is an online auction held in early November through Real Auction.

How often does Mesa County reappraise homes?

Real property is reappraised in odd-numbered years, and the value generally carries into the even-numbered year after.

Can I postpone my Mesa County property taxes?

The Treasurer runs a Property Tax Deferral Program that postpones payment in exchange for a recorded lien. Ask the office whether you qualify, and expect the lien to be cleared when you sell.

Douglas County at a glance

South of Denver, Douglas County stretches across about 843 square miles around its seat, Castle Rock. Population went from 357,978 in 2020 to an estimated 399,396 in 2025. Highlands Ranch is the biggest community, and Parker, Lone Tree, Castle Pines and Castle Rock appear on bills too. Littleton and Aurora each overlap a slice of the county.

Mesas, foothills, small streams and ponderosa pine shape flood zones, wildfire exposure and lot values. A lot that backs onto open space, a creek or a forested slope may draw an insurance quote that moves the offer, whereas a cash buyer doesn't have to wait on one.

Who handles property tax

One office sets value, another collects. The Assessor sits at 301 Wilcox Street in Castle Rock, open weekdays 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., phone 303-660-7450. The county main line is 303-660-7400.

On the Treasurer's website, an interactive "Where do my taxes go?" map lays out the taxing authorities and total mill levy for your district designation. Since totals depend on the designation, neighbors can pay different amounts.

How Colorado values a Douglas County home

Colorado prices a home from comparable sales, then layers on an assessment rate and the local mill levy. The sequence runs classification, actual value, assessed value, tax rate.

Residential property has used two assessment rates since 2025, one for local governments and one for schools, and the 2026 chart shows 6.8% and 7.05%. Sales for tax years 2025 and 2026 come from January 1, 2023 through June 30, 2024, with earlier periods used if data is thin. Your own bill will differ with your levy. The revenue stays in the county and supports schools, counties, special districts, municipalities and junior colleges.

Valuation notices and objections

The county sends Notices of Value on May 1, and you have until June 8 to object in writing, by mail or online. Online booking is available for in-person meetings. Appeals on business personal property open June 15 and close June 30 by delivery or postmark.

Only properties with a change in value, use or ownership get a notice, which the county says is fewer than 10% of owners. If you didn't get one, your value probably carried forward.

A step-by-step path for a Douglas County seller

Selling with a tax question hanging over the house is manageable if you take it in order.

  1. Check your Notice of Value in May. If you disagree, file by June 8.
  2. Look up your district designation on the Treasurer's map, so you know which authorities and what total mill levy apply to the parcel.
  3. Confirm which payments you have made: first half by the end of February, second half by June 15, or the single April 30 payment.
  4. Ask the Treasurer for a current payoff before you accept an offer, and share it with the buyer and the title company.
  5. At closing, the title company pays any balance from your proceeds and the sale proceeds from there.

Keep each receipt, so you can show the title company which payments are already made. A sale in the middle of the year means your title officer can match those against the payoff.

Reading your valuation notice

Check your Notice of Value against recent sales near you. For tax years 2025 and 2026 the comparable sales window runs from January 1, 2023 through June 30, 2024. If the notice lists details that are wrong, say so in your objection, since a corrected record is a fair reason to object alongside the question of value.

Mail your objection so it is postmarked by June 8, or file online. If you would rather talk it through, book an in-person meeting online. If you did not get a notice at all, your value probably carried forward from the year before.

If the appeal is denied

A denial isn't the end. The Board of Equalization is the next level up, and it owes you a written decision within five business days. After that, you get 30 days from the mailing to take the dispute to an arbitrator, district court or the state Board of Assessment Appeals.

Counties over 300,000 residents must use the alternate schedule. Douglas County had 357,978 residents in 2020, so ask the Assessor which column applies to your notice.

In plain terms, the year runs like this: notices in early May, objections by June 8, a Notice of Determination from the Assessor, then the Board of Equalization if you want to push further. An appeal that is still open when you list is worth telling your buyer about, because a successful one lowers the bill for whoever owns the house next. Keep your filing confirmation and any evidence you sent in the same folder as your closing papers.

Tax relief programs

Several statewide programs are open to Douglas County owners:

  • Property tax, rent and heat rebate.
  • Property tax deferral.
  • Work-off program.
  • Senior property tax exemption.
  • Veteran with a disability exemption.

Call the state Division of Property Taxation at (303) 864-7777. The state sets applications and deadlines, so ask before you list; a seller who qualifies may owe less than the bill suggests.

When taxes go unpaid

Each November the Treasurer holds an internet sale of tax liens, with interest at 13%, which is nine points over the federal discount rate as of September 1. Buyers get a lien rather than the house, and fewer than 1 percent of purchases end in a deed transfer.

  • Delinquent notices are mailed in July.
  • The lien sale is the last step for most accounts.
  • A lien investor collects interest from the owner.
  • Paying before the sale avoids that interest.

If you are behind and thinking of selling, the clock matters. Tax debt grows while you wait for a traditional listing to find a buyer.

Handling property tax when you sell

Get a current balance, confirm which half-year payments are made, and let the closing agent pay the rest from your proceeds. Payments normally fall at the end of February and June 15 for halves, or April 30 for the full amount.

  • Keep your statement and payment receipts for both halves.
  • Check Notices of Value each May, because a protest affects the next bill.
  • Ask about senior and veteran exemptions if they apply to you.

A tax-delinquent house, an inherited house or a rental with a code problem is what many sellers here bring to a cash buyer. On that route the balance is still paid at closing, and the house sells as it stands without repairs or showings.

Whichever route you choose, the same three questions apply: what do you owe now, which payments are already made, and is any appeal still open. Having those answers before the first offer keeps the closing date from slipping.

What is the Douglas County property tax appeal deadline?

June 8 for real property objections, by mail or online. Notices of Value are released May 1.

Where is the Douglas County Assessor's office?

301 Wilcox Street, Castle Rock. Hours are Monday to Friday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., and the phone is 303-660-7450.

When is the Douglas County tax lien sale?

It is held online each November, and the interest rate is 13%.

Is Castle Rock the county seat?

Yes. The seat moved to Castle Rock in 1874, and the Assessor and other county offices now sit on Wilcox Street there.
